_meta.tier_note: trend is real; findings each carry their own data_tier; bikeway_mileage and protected_share are derived.

caveats.text: Crash counts are raw, not normalized by ridership (no public cyclist-volume data is joined yet), so busy corridors look worse than dangerous quiet ones.
Recent months are provisional — crash records get amended upstream, so the most recent 1-2 months of any trend may still move.
Dooring crashes are structurally undercounted in police crash reports (see the dooring-undercount finding).

trend.note: Monthly counts of police-reported cyclist crashes citywide since Sept 2017; ksi = crashes whose worst injury was fatal or incapacitating ("killed or seriously injured"). Recent months are provisional — records get amended.

findings.title: Cyclists killed or seriously injured
findings.description: A cyclist was killed or seriously injured ("incapacitating" in police records) in 217 crashes in the 12 months through 2026-07-20, vs 165 the prior 12 months. Vision Zero's goal is zero.
findings.caveat: Counts, not rates — ridership growth is not netted out. Recent months are provisional.

findings.title: How much of the network protects riders
findings.description: Only 15% of Chicago's 446 on-street bikeway miles are physically protected lanes (69 mi); counting buffered lanes brings it to 39%. The rest is paint, sharrows, and greenways. Off-street trails are tracked separately.
findings.caveat: Share of current on-street network mileage as of 2026-07-22; protected = barrier/curb-protected on-street lanes. Off-street trails are excluded — they live in the separate OSM layer.

findings.title: How much of the street grid has bike infrastructure
findings.description: Chicago has 3,944 miles of surface streets (arterials, collectors, and neighborhood streets). 446 miles — 11% — have any bike infrastructure at all, counting everything from sharrows to protected lanes.
findings.caveat: Centerline miles on both sides of the ratio. Expressways, ramps, alleys, and river channels are excluded from street miles; off-street trails are excluded from bikeway miles. The street centerline layer was last updated in 2021 — the grid changes slowly.

findings.title: Highest crash-density corridors
findings.description: Top corridors by cyclist crashes per km of bikeway: Kinzie (77.46/km); Wells (51.67/km); Clark (45.84/km); Milwaukee (43.02/km); Dearborn (37.44/km).
findings.caveat: Raw counts, not normalized by bike volume. Dooring is undercounted. Per-km rates inflate short segments — Kinzie's rate rides on very few km.

findings.title: How often the driver leaves
findings.description: In 27% of police-reported cyclist crashes since Sept 2017 (4667 of 17356), the driver left the scene — 27% when the cyclist was injured.
findings.caveat: Share of reported crashes; unreported crashes are not counted.

findings.title: Ward concentration
findings.description: 5 of 50 wards account for 27% of located cyclist crashes since Sept 2017: Ward 27 (1197), Ward 42 (1105), Ward 32 (822), Ward 1 (819), Ward 34 (661).
findings.caveat: Ward totals reflect where people ride most, not only where streets are worst.

findings.title: Dooring: structurally undercounted
findings.description: 2040 crashes since Sept 2017 carry a dooring flag. Dooring is structurally excluded from 'reportable' crash records unless damage/injury thresholds are met, so the real number is higher than any count on this site.
findings.caveat: A floor, not a full count.

findings.title: How Chicago's bike network scores nationally
findings.description: PeopleForBikes' Bicycle Network Analysis scores how much of Chicago a person can reach on low-stress streets — and gives the city 11.08 out of 100. The average rated U.S. city scores 36. Among the 73 rated U.S. cities over 300,000 people, Chicago ranks last. Behind the number: 6,267 miles of high-stress streets versus 1,834 low-stress. That's up slightly from 9 in 2024. This grades the network, not crashes: it can move independently of any crash trend, because it measures what's built, not what happened.
findings.caveat: Third-party score, analysis 26.05 (May 2026). Computed by PeopleForBikes from OpenStreetMap — only as current as volunteer mapping, which is uneven across neighborhoods; it can understate what a neighborhood has, or miss hazards nobody mapped. PFB's scoring methodology has changed over the years (notably 2020 and 2026), so history entries are not comparable across distant analysis versions. It grades the street network, not the people riding it — a low score is a case for building more, not a reason not to ride.

findings.title: Promised bikeway miles vs. what got built
findings.description: CDOT's 2023 Chicago Cycling Strategy commits to 150 miles of new bikeways, 80% of them low-stress. Using CDOT's own year-by-year installation figures (2023–2025), the city has built 103.8 miles of genuinely new bikeway — 69% of the pledge. CDOT itself reports 125.9 miles (84%) toward the same goal, but 22.0 of those miles are concrete upgrades to protected lanes that already existed, not new bikeway. On the low-stress pledge, 80.3% of the miles CDOT counts are low-stress; counting only genuinely new miles, 76.2%. Source: Chicago Department of Transportation, 2023 Chicago Cycling Strategy; installation figures from CDOT FOIA S145367-071326, released 2026-07-24.
findings.caveat: Both figures come from CDOT's own Complete Streets dashboard, so the gap is a counting difference, not a dispute about the underlying miles. The pledge says "new bikeways," which is why the headline excludes the 22.0 miles of concrete upgrades; CDOT's larger number is shown alongside so both countings are visible. Low-stress here means protected lanes, neighborhood greenways, and off-street trails — buffered and painted lanes and sharrows are excluded, the same way this site's network map grades them, and the same way CDOT's own dashboard counts them. The pledge carries no published deadline, so this is progress-to-date, not a verdict on whether CDOT will meet it.

bikeway_mileage.note: Citywide on-street bikeway miles by facility type, 2010 to 2026-07-22. Years 2010-2025 are CDOT's own year-end figures from the Complete Streets dashboard released under FOIA S145367-071326; later points are OYL snapshots of the public CDOT Bike Routes layer. Both are centerline miles and agree to 0.03 mi where they overlap. The series is on-street only: the public layer omits off-street trails, so they are carried separately in `off_street` for the years CDOT reported them and are null for snapshots. Facility mix changes between years can reflect upgrades (a buffered lane rebuilt as protected) as well as new construction.

protected_share.note: Protected share of on-street bikeway miles; excludes off-street trails.
